ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Here the graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is contextual: in the recurring pair "this thing is mind; outside mind no thing stands; this mind is the thing; outside it no mind stands" (此法即心，心外無法；此心即法，法外無心), it names what could be set up as a thing apart, not an untranslated religious loanword.
EvidenceBody: Shao's frequently quoted verse places the phrase beside visible landscape: "the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes" (通玄峰頂，不是人間；心外無法，滿目青山). A later master quotes that verse and says it has been "broken into two pieces" (打成兩橛). Another hall address strikes the Chan seat and asks: "mind has not arisen—where could the things be established? Where did mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?" (心既不生，法從何立？山河大地，甚處得來). The corpus therefore records the line as a maxim, a verse, a question to the assembly, and an object of later criticism; this entry does not decide the criticism.
